title: Safety: bias, red teaming, failure disclosure
story:
Start with where it comes from, because the usual framing — that a model might pick up bias somewhere — is too vague to act on. Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan showed in 2017 that applying machine learning to ordinary human language results in human-like semantic biases: using a widely used, purely statistical model trained on a standard corpus of text from the web, they replicated a spectrum of known biases as measured by the Implicit Association Test. Their conclusion is that text corpora contain recoverable and accurate imprints of historic biases, from the morally neutral, such as preferring flowers to insects, to problematic ones regarding race or gender.

Read that as a statement about the material rather than about any model. The associations are in the text because they are in the writing of the people who produced it, and a system trained to predict that text learns them along with everything else it learns. Nothing went wrong in training. There is no bug. The model absorbed what was there, which is exactly what it was built to do.

Two consequences follow immediately. The first is that a system does not become biased through misuse — it arrives that way, and neutrality is a property you would have to add rather than a default you can preserve. The second is that measurement has to be specific: the same paper applies a stated test to stated groups of words, and that specificity is what makes it a finding rather than an opinion. The authors also flag their own caveat, that the corpora are uncontrolled and not representative of any one population, which precludes direct numerical comparison with human results. Notice a strong result carrying its own limit, because that is the standard to copy.

So measure your own system in the same spirit, and accept the narrowness. Choose the groups that matter for what you are building — names, places, dialects, whatever your users actually differ by — write inputs that vary only that attribute, and compare the outputs. Does the refusal rate change? Does the tone? Does the assumed context? The test you build measures what you thought to test, and a clean result means those particular comparisons on those particular inputs came out even. It does not mean the system is fair, and describing it that way is how a measurement becomes a marketing claim.

Red teaming is the other half, and it answers a different question. Evaluation asks whether the system still does what you meant on cases you wrote. Red teaming asks what somebody trying to get a bad outcome can make it do, which requires adversarial intent rather than coverage. Give people time to attack it deliberately, include people who are not on the team, write down everything that worked, and convert each success into a case that stays in the suite. The first session always finds more than anyone expects, which is itself the argument for having one.

Then the part nobody enjoys, which is what you do with what you learn. Failures found and not written down are failures that will be found again, by someone with less patience and a wider audience. Tell users plainly what the system is not good at, what it will not do, and what has been found to go wrong — in the product where they can see it, not in a document nobody opens. And when something does go wrong in front of a user, say what happened and what changed, because the alternative is a user who has learned that your system fails silently and that you do not mention it.

None of this is a compliance exercise, and treating it as one produces documents rather than safety. The practical version is small and it is a habit: know that the biases in your training material are in your system, measure a few specific things you actually care about, attack it on purpose before somebody else does, and be honest about the limits in public. That is available to a team of one, it costs a few days a quarter, and it is the difference between a system whose failures are known and a system whose failures are merely undiscovered.

problem.name: Finding harms before your users do
problem.shape: A system trained on human material carries what was in that material, and nobody has looked for it.
tell: fairness is asserted rather than measured on stated groups
nobody outside the team has attacked the system deliberately
findings from an adversarial session were discussed and not written into the suite
the known limitations live in a document rather than in the product
problem.move: Assume the associations in the training material are present in the system, measure specific comparisons on groups that matter to your users, run deliberate adversarial sessions with outsiders, convert every success into a permanent case, and state the limits where users can see them.
problem.invariant: Text corpora contain recoverable imprints of historic bias, so a model trained to predict that text carries them by construction rather than through any defect in training.
problem.breaks: A measurement only covers the groups and comparisons you chose, so a clean result means those inputs came out even and says nothing about fairness in general.

cost.time: adversarial sessions and comparison suites are human work that cannot be automated away
cost.space: every finding becomes a permanent case, which grows the suite and is the point of the exercise
cost.beats: asserting fairness, which cannot be checked, and waiting for users to find the failures, which they will do publicly

problem.practice: Take twenty real inputs and produce a second copy of each that differs only in a name, a place or a dialect. Run both sets and compare refusal rates, tone and assumed context. Whatever you find, you now have a measurement rather than an assurance — and a suite you can re-run on every change.

beats.broke: Text corpora carry recoverable imprints of historic bias, so a model trained to predict that text arrives carrying them, with nothing having gone wrong in training.
beats.fix: Measure specific comparisons on groups that matter, attack the system deliberately with people from outside the team, turn every success into a permanent case, and disclose the limits in the product.
beats.cost: The measurement only covers what you thought to test, and the work is human time that cannot be automated away.
